claims.text: The as-cast Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy contains several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
The alloy undergoes a complex, multistep crystallization sequence during solidification.
The proposed intervention is to apply several GPa of pressure during rapid cooling immediately after melting.
A cooling rate above 10^4 K/s is tentatively identified as exceeding the alloy's critical cooling-rate threshold.
Significant crystallization normally occurs under the proposed rapid-cooling conditions.
High pressure suppresses nucleation sites for the primary crystalline phases.
High pressure increases the alloy's effective viscosity.
High pressure raises the nucleation-energy barrier.
High pressure increases the activation energy for atomic rearrangements leading to crystallization.
The increased activation energy delays nucleation and growth of primary crystalline phases during solidification and reheating.
Delayed nucleation and growth promote formation and retention of an amorphous structure.
Relative to ambient-pressure processing, high-pressure processing will shift crystallization onset to higher temperatures during reheating.
High-pressure processing will reduce the fraction of primary crystalline phases formed under slower cooling.
High-pressure processing will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
Conventional rapid cooling at ambient pressure produces extensive primary non-eutectic crystallization and limited amorphous retention.
The intervention is effective only when cooling exceeds a tentative threshold of 10^4 K/s.
The intervention is effective on reheating only below an unspecified temperature at which pressure effects diminish.
There is no direct prior evidence for the proposed intervention in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome extends the benefit to slower cooling, whereas the boundary states that the intervention is effective only above a rapid-cooling threshold tentatively set at 10^4 K/s.

The intervention applies pressure only during rapid cooling, but the mechanism and boundary invoke direct pressure-dependent suppression during subsequent reheating without stating that pressure is maintained during reheating or explaining a persistent post-processing effect.
